---
title: "Neighborhoods"
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    collapse: true
    comment: "#>"
    message: false
---

`spatial_similarity()` counts how often labels neighbor one another, so the
result depends on which spots or cells count as neighbors. There are three
ways to define a neighborhood:

- `"radius"`: all spots/cells within `radius`.
- `"knn"`: the `k` nearest. Neighborhoods are symmetric, so a spot/cell can
  have more than `k` neighbors when it is among the nearest of others.
- `"delaunay"`: the spots/cells surrounding each one, by Delaunay
  triangulation, ignoring links longer than `radius`.

By default (`"auto"`), `"radius"` is used for positions on a grid and
`"delaunay"` otherwise. The plots below, from `plot_neighborhoods()`, show
the same generated tissue section, with holes and a narrow tear, as spots or
cells, and each definition with a few parameter choices: each highlighted spot
or cell has its own color, with its neighbors in a lighter shade. To check the
neighborhoods in your own data, call `plot_neighborhoods()` with the same
`samples`, `neighborhood`, `radius` and `k` as `spatial_similarity()`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-setup
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup"
library(friendlycells)

# Whether positions, in multiples of the spacing, lie in a generated section
in_tissue <- function(u, v) {
  theta <- atan2(v, u)
  edge <- 16 * (1 + 0.3 * cos(2 * theta) + 0.1 * sin(3 * theta) +
    0.05 * cos(5 * theta + 1))
  inside <- sqrt(u^2 + v^2) < edge
  holes <- rbind(
    c(0, 14, 6), c(-11, 3, 2.5), c(-5, -4, 1.5), c(2, 4, 2), c(8, -2, 1.2),
    c(14, 5, 2), c(-16, -3, 1.5), c(4, -9, 1.2), c(-7, 8, 1.2), c(9, 8, 1.5),
    c(-1, -10, 1), c(17, -3, 1.2), c(-13, -9, 1)
  )
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(holes))) {
    inside <- inside &
      sqrt((u - holes[i, 1])^2 + (v - holes[i, 2])^2) > holes[i, 3]
  }
  # A tear
  inside & !(abs(v - 0.4 * u + 6) < 0.6 & u < -3)
}
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-setup
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from friendlycells import plot_neighborhoods


def in_tissue(u, v):
    """Whether positions, in multiples of the spacing, lie in a generated section."""
    theta = np.arctan2(v, u)
    edge = 16 * (
        1 + 0.3 * np.cos(2 * theta) + 0.1 * np.sin(3 * theta)
        + 0.05 * np.cos(5 * theta + 1)
    )
    inside = np.hypot(u, v) < edge
    holes = [
        (0, 14, 6), (-11, 3, 2.5), (-5, -4, 1.5), (2, 4, 2), (8, -2, 1.2),
        (14, 5, 2), (-16, -3, 1.5), (4, -9, 1.2), (-7, 8, 1.2), (9, 8, 1.5),
        (-1, -10, 1), (17, -3, 1.2), (-13, -9, 1),
    ]
    for hole_u, hole_v, hole_r in holes:
        inside &= np.hypot(u - hole_u, v - hole_v) > hole_r
    # A tear
    return inside & ~((np.abs(v - 0.4 * u + 6) < 0.6) & (u < -3))
```
:::

## Hexagonal grid

Visium spots lie on a hexagonal grid, 100 µm apart.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-hex-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the spots"
rows <- expand.grid(col = -60:60, row = -40:40)
rows <- rows[(rows$col + rows$row) %% 2 == 0, ]
# plot_neighborhoods() needs a label column, but doesn't use it
hex <- data.frame(x = 50 * rows$col, y = 50 * sqrt(3) * rows$row, label = "")
hex <- hex[in_tissue(hex$x / 100, hex$y / 100), ]
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-hex-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the spots"
col, row = np.meshgrid(np.arange(-60, 61), np.arange(-40, 41))
keep = (col + row) % 2 == 0
x, y = 50 * col[keep], 50 * np.sqrt(3) * row[keep]
keep = in_tissue(x / 100, y / 100)
# plot_neighborhoods() needs a label column, but doesn't use it
hex_grid = pd.DataFrame({"x": x[keep], "y": y[keep], "label": ""})
```
:::

### Radius

The default radius (120 µm, 1.2 times the spacing) gives each spot its six
immediate neighbors, and larger radii add further rings, but spots at edges
and holes have fewer.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-hex-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 120 (default)" = hex), neighborhood = "radius")
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 180" = hex), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 180)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 210" = hex), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 210)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-hex-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 120 (default)": hex_grid}, neighborhood="radius")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 180": hex_grid}, neighborhood="radius", radius=180)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 210": hex_grid}, neighborhood="radius", radius=210)
plt.show()
```
:::

### k nearest neighbors

`k = 6` gives the same six as the default radius away from edges, but other
values of `k` have to choose between spots at the same distance, so they
choose arbitrarily. At edges, `"knn"` reaches further to make up `k`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-hex-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 4" = hex), neighborhood = "knn", k = 4)
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 6 (default)" = hex), neighborhood = "knn")
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 8" = hex), neighborhood = "knn", k = 8)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-hex-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 4": hex_grid}, neighborhood="knn", k=4)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 6 (default)": hex_grid}, neighborhood="knn")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 8": hex_grid}, neighborhood="knn", k=8)
plt.show()
```
:::

### Delaunay

Delaunay triangulation also gives the six immediate neighbors away from edges,
but links spots across holes and the tear. Its `radius` limits how far:
150 µm stops these links, the default (300 µm, 3 times the spacing) keeps
those across small holes, and with no radius every link is kept.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-hex-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 150" = hex), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = 150)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 300 (default)" = hex), neighborhood = "delaunay")
plot_neighborhoods(list("no radius" = hex), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = Inf)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-hex-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 150": hex_grid}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=150)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 300 (default)": hex_grid}, neighborhood="delaunay")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"no radius": hex_grid}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=np.inf)
plt.show()
```
:::

## Square grid

Visium HD bins lie on a square grid, here of 8 µm bins, so the section is
much smaller than on the hexagonal grid.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-square-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the bins"
square <- data.frame(expand.grid(x = 8 * -30:30, y = 8 * -30:30), label = "")
square <- square[in_tissue(square$x / 8, square$y / 8), ]
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-square-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the bins"
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(-30, 31), np.arange(-30, 31))
keep = in_tissue(x, y)
square = pd.DataFrame({"x": 8 * x[keep], "y": 8 * y[keep], "label": ""})
```
:::

### Radius

The default radius (9.6 µm) gives each bin its four side neighbors, 12 µm
(1.5 times the bin size) adds the four diagonals, and 17 µm adds the next bin
along each side. Bins at edges and holes have fewer.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-square-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 9.6 (default)" = square), neighborhood = "radius")
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 12" = square), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 12)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 17" = square), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 17)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-square-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 9.6 (default)": square}, neighborhood="radius")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 12": square}, neighborhood="radius", radius=12)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 17": square}, neighborhood="radius", radius=17)
plt.show()
```
:::

### k nearest neighbors

Away from edges, `k = 4` and `k = 8` give the same neighbors as the first two
radii, but `k = 6` has to choose between the four diagonals, so it chooses
arbitrarily. At edges, `"knn"` reaches further to make up `k`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-square-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 4" = square), neighborhood = "knn", k = 4)
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 6 (default)" = square), neighborhood = "knn")
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 8" = square), neighborhood = "knn", k = 8)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-square-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 4": square}, neighborhood="knn", k=4)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 6 (default)": square}, neighborhood="knn")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 8": square}, neighborhood="knn", k=8)
plt.show()
```
:::

### Delaunay

Delaunay triangulation splits each square into two triangles along an
arbitrary diagonal. A `radius` of 10 µm drops the diagonals, leaving the four
side neighbors, but then `"delaunay"` is the same as the default `"radius"`;
with larger radii the diagonals are arbitrary and links cross gaps, so avoid
`"delaunay"` for bins.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-square-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 10" = square), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = 10)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 24 (default)" = square), neighborhood = "delaunay")
plot_neighborhoods(list("no radius" = square), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = Inf)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-square-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 10": square}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=10)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 24 (default)": square}, neighborhood="delaunay")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"no radius": square}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=np.inf)
plt.show()
```
:::

## Segmented cells

Segmented cells (Xenium, or Visium HD with cell segmentation) are unevenly
spaced. These cells are generated in the same section, sparser on the left
than on the right: typically 9 µm from their nearest neighbor on the left, and
6.5 µm on the right.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-segmented-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the cells"
set.seed(1)
cells <- NULL
for (step in c(1.2, 0.85)) {
  grid <- expand.grid(u = seq(-30, 30, step), v = seq(-30, 30, step))
  u <- grid$u + runif(nrow(grid), -0.3, 0.3) * step
  v <- grid$v + runif(nrow(grid), -0.3, 0.3) * step
  # Sparser on the left than on the right
  keep <- in_tissue(u, v) & (u < 0) == (step > 1)
  cells <- rbind(cells, data.frame(x = 10 * u[keep], y = 10 * v[keep], label = ""))
}
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-segmented-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Generate the cells"
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
parts = []
for step in [1.2, 0.85]:
    u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(-30, 30, step), np.arange(-30, 30, step))
    u = u.ravel() + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, u.size) * step
    v = v.ravel() + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, v.size) * step
    # Sparser on the left than on the right
    keep = in_tissue(u, v) & ((u < 0) == (step > 1))
    parts.append(pd.DataFrame({"x": 10 * u[keep], "y": 10 * v[keep], "label": ""}))
cells = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
```
:::

### Radius

No radius suits every cell: one that links the dense cells leaves sparse cells
with few neighbors or none, while one that links the sparse cells gives dense
cells many.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-segmented-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 10" = cells), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 10)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 15" = cells), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 15)
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 20" = cells), neighborhood = "radius", radius = 20)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-segmented-radius
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 10": cells}, neighborhood="radius", radius=10)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 15": cells}, neighborhood="radius", radius=15)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 20": cells}, neighborhood="radius", radius=20)
plt.show()
```
:::

### k nearest neighbors

`"knn"` gives every cell at least `k` neighbors, however far away they are.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-segmented-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 4" = cells), neighborhood = "knn", k = 4)
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 6 (default)" = cells), neighborhood = "knn")
plot_neighborhoods(list("k = 8" = cells), neighborhood = "knn", k = 8)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-segmented-knn
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 4": cells}, neighborhood="knn", k=4)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 6 (default)": cells}, neighborhood="knn")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"k = 8": cells}, neighborhood="knn", k=8)
plt.show()
```
:::

### Delaunay

`"delaunay"` links each cell to the cells around it, whatever their spacing.
Its `radius` (by default 3 times the typical spacing, about 21 µm) only drops
links across gaps, such as holes.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-segmented-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
plot_neighborhoods(list("radius = 12" = cells), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = 12)
plot_neighborhoods(list("default radius" = cells), neighborhood = "delaunay")
plot_neighborhoods(list("no radius" = cells), neighborhood = "delaunay", radius = Inf)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-segmented-delaunay
#| layout-ncol: 3
plot_neighborhoods({"radius = 12": cells}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=12)
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"default radius": cells}, neighborhood="delaunay")
plt.show()
plot_neighborhoods({"no radius": cells}, neighborhood="delaunay", radius=np.inf)
plt.show()
```
:::
